Culpable

/KUL-puh-bul/ — stress on KUL · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Culpable describes someone who deserves blame for having done something wrong.

The report found the shipping company culpable for the oil spill.

Worked Example

The principal determined that the student was culpable for the incident, despite his insistence that he was just following orders.

Culpa is Latin for blame or fault (as in 'mea culpa,' my fault). Culpa + -able (worthy of) = worthy of blame, deserving censure. This is a rule-breaker: Latin culpabilis already ended in -abilis, and English kept the -a instead of switching to -ible. The scenario shows the student bears fault (culpa) for the wrongdoing—he cannot escape culpability by blaming obedience.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

responsible: Responsible means answerable for something — you caused it or it was yours to handle — and the word can stay neutral, even positive. Culpable never stays neutral: it says the person deserves blame for a wrong. A driver is responsible for a fender-bender; a drunk driver is culpable.

liable: Liable means legally answerable for wrongdoing or damage — a courtroom word about who must pay or answer under the law. Culpable is a moral judgment that needs no court: it says the person deserves the blame. A company can be liable without any employee being personally culpable.

guilty: Guilty means established to have committed the offense — a verdict, an admission, the deed pinned to the doer. Culpable is about deserving blame, which can be a matter of degree before anything is established. A suspect may be partly culpable long before any court finds them guilty.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

innocent: free of guilt or wrongdoing

blameless: deserving no blame at all

Where it sits · how much blame is deserved — careless → irresponsible → negligent → culpable

careless vs. culpable: A careless student forgets small things, but a culpable one deserves real blame for the harm that was done.

irresponsible vs. culpable: An irresponsible driver ignores the rules, while a culpable one is judged to deserve the blame for the crash.

negligent vs. culpable: A negligent guard fails in a serious duty, but a culpable one is found to deserve the blame for what happened outright.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — culp(a)

Root — culp(a): blame, fault — as in the classic apology 'mea culpa,' literally 'my fault' (Latin)

Suffix — -able

Suffix — -able: able to be; here shading toward 'deserving of' (Latin (-abilis))

Put it together

Put it together: culpa ('blame') + -able = able to be blamed. Notice how -able shades here from 'can be' to 'deserves to be': someone culpable doesn't just happen to get blamed — they deserve the blame for having done something wrong.

Use the root in a new word: culprit

Use the root in a new word: culprit: The detective finally identified the culprit who had been leaving muddy footprints in the hallway.

Word Choice

formal

Reach for culpable when assigning blame for a specific wrong. Unlike 'responsible' (which can be neutral), culpable always carries a moral judgment of wrongdoing. Use it in legal, ethical, or serious interpersonal contexts where fault and blameworthiness are at issue.
